messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL exactly matches the DOI given in the source: “10.1016/j.jwpe.2025.107875” and the same URL string is shown.

The experiments mix multiple matrices (Milli-Q, groundwater, wastewater) and multiple adsorbents (AC and BC-W) while reporting combined adsorption capacities “across all tested matrices” (S13-E03). This justifies classifying the data as descriptive_only for cross-study quantitative comparison.

The stated reason—that capacities are summarized across matrices/adsorbents and that wastewater organic matter affects performance—is consistent with S13-E03, which notes decreased adsorption in wastewater due to organic matter competition and gives single capacity values “across all tested matrices.”
S13-E05 and S13-E07 describe adsorption isotherms of PFAS onto AC and BC-W and discuss adsorption capacity; this is correctly classified as a sorption endpoint.

Batch adsorption isotherms and adsorption capacity in mg g−1 are explicitly described (S13-E05, S13-E07), matching the interpretation that this is the amount sorbed per mass of adsorbent at equilibrium.
S13-E04 reports percentage removal (100%, 82%, 60%) and S13-E03 discusses PFAS removal effectiveness across matrices; these are removal endpoints.

S13-E03 notes PFAS removal remained effective in Milli-Q water and groundwater but decreased in wastewater due to organic matter competition, while S13-E04 provides removal percentages, matching the interpretation.

The third endpoint summarizes mechanistic interpretation (hydrophobic interactions, chain length, DOM competition) rather than a measured performance metric; classifying it as “other” is appropriate and supported by S13-E02, S13-E05, S13-E07, and S13-E03.

S13-E05 and S13-E02 attribute adsorption trends to hydrophobicity, chain length, and functional group; S13-E07 emphasizes hydrophobic interactions; S13-E03 attributes wastewater performance decrease to organic matter competition, especially for PFOA—all matching the stated interpretation.

S13-E03 provides single adsorption capacity values (7.7, 16.1, 4.8 mg g−1) “across all tested matrices” for AC and BC-W, without matrix- or adsorbent-specific breakdown. It is a valid design-inferred limitation that this constrains matrix- and material-specific interpretation.

S13-E03 qualitatively attributes decreased wastewater performance to organic matter competition, particularly for PFOA, and mentions co-contaminants and natural organic matter, but no quantitative competitive-adsorption parameters are given in the supplied text. The stated design-inferred limitation follows.

S13-E01 refers to “PFAS-concentrated water matrices, including groundwater and waste-water,” and S13-E03 states that PFAS removal remained effective in “Milli-Q water and groundwater” but decreased in wastewater. Together they support the value listing Milli-Q water, groundwater, and wastewater.
S13-E02 and S13-E08 specify that the dose of each adsorbent was 1 g L−1; S13-E07 repeats “using 1 g L−1 of adsorbent,” matching the value 1.
The unit g L−1 is explicitly used in S13-E02, S13-E07, and S13-E08 for adsorbent dose and is correctly recorded as g/L.
S13-E05 states that adsorption isotherms were conducted over a concentration range of 0.1 to 100 mg L−1 of each PFAS, matching the value 0.1–100.
S13-E05 gives the concentration range in mg L−1; recording the unit as mg/L is correct.
S13-E05 notes Cd(II) was maintained at a constant 10 mg L−1 while PFAS concentration varied, matching the value 10.
Cd(II) concentration is reported in mg L−1 in S13-E05, so mg/L is the correct unit.
S13-E07 specifies isotherm experiments used 24 h of contact time, matching the value 24.
Contact time is clearly expressed in hours (24 h) in S13-E07, so unit h is correct.
Both S13-E02 (kinetics) and S13-E07 (isotherms) give pH ~7, matching the value “~7.”
pH is dimensionless and rightly has a null/empty unit; the text (S13-E02, S13-E07) only gives a numeric pH value.

S13-E03 attributes decreased wastewater adsorption performance to organic matter competition and mentions co-contaminants, co-occurring cations, and natural organic matter. This supports the description of dissolved organic matter and co-occurring cations as co-constituents.
The co-constituents field is descriptive and not quantitative; having no unit is appropriate and consistent with the source.
S13-E01 lists perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) with its formula, matching the value.
S13-E01 lists perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) with its formula, matching the value.
S13-E01 lists perfluoro-2-propoxypropanoic acid (GenX), matching the value.
S13-E03 reports [SOURCE_TEXT_OMITTED sha256=3b01d9c4214a0f07ca1456189a3a2f46851077e10b27fd9e8373d33f078e6582].” The first value 7.7 corresponds to PFOA and is correctly transcribed.
S13-E03 reports capacities in mg g−1; mg/g is the correct unit.
The second capacity reported in S13-E03 is 16.1 mg g−1 for PFOS, matching the value 16.1.
The adsorption capacity unit given in S13-E03 is mg g−1; mg/g is correctly recorded.
The third capacity in S13-E03 is 4.8 mg g−1 for GenX, matching the value 4.8.
Again, S13-E03 uses mg g−1 for adsorption capacity; mg/g is correct.

The supplied text (methods, results, and conclusion excerpts) discuss only adsorption of PFAS and Cd(II) and do not mention degradation, transformation products, or defluorination; inferring that only mass transfer (adsorption) was studied is reasonable as a design-inferred statement.

S13-E08 describes batch experiments in 50-mL bottles with 20 mg adsorbent and 20 mL solution (1 g L−1) and S13-E03 mentions tests in multiple water matrices, indicating bench-scale batch adsorption isotherms and multi-matrix tests with AC and biochars for PFAS and Cd(II) removal.
The work describes new batch adsorption experiments with specified methods and results (S13-E08, S13-E05, S13-E03), which is a primary experimental study.

S13-E01 and S13-E08 describe commercial activated carbon and several biochars (including wood-derived BC-W) used as adsorbents for PFAS and Cd(II) in batch adsorption experiments; S13-E03 and the title emphasize simultaneous PFAS and Cd(II) removal and regeneration, matching the description of regenerable carbonaceous adsorbents AC and BC-W evaluated across matrices.

result.record_usable_rationale: All core elements—study identity, matrices, adsorbents, operating conditions, endpoints (adsorption and removal), and quantitative adsorption capacities—are accurately transcribed and well supported by the cited source text. Any interpretive or limitation statements are clearly design-inferred and consistent with the evidence, so the record is suitable for synthesis with attention to its descriptive-only comparability status.
